lessons.title: The Podcast That Killed the Radio Star

script.speaker: Host
script.line: Welcome back to the segment, where today we're diving into something a bit nostalgic: the slow fade of terrestrial radio.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: For decades, radio was the beating heart of popular culture — the place you'd hear a song for the first time, or catch breaking news mid-commute.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: Now, podcasts have muscled their way in, and frankly, they've eaten radio's lunch in more ways than one.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: There's something almost paradoxical about it, though. Podcasts are essentially radio's format — spoken audio, delivered episodically — just untethered from a broadcast schedule.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: What radio had going for it was spontaneity. A DJ riffing live, reacting to a caller, or breaking into a show with urgent news.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: Podcasts, by contrast, are polished, edited, often recorded days or weeks in advance. You lose that live-wire unpredictability.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: But you gain intimacy. A host talking into a mic for ninety minutes, unhurried, feels more like a conversation with a mate than a broadcast to millions.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: That intimacy is precisely why advertisers have piled into the space — listeners trust the voice in their ear far more than a jingle between songs.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: Still, I'd argue radio isn't dead so much as it's been forced to specialize. Live traffic updates, local call-in shows, community stations — that's radio's remaining turf.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: And ironically, plenty of radio veterans have jumped ship to podcasting themselves, chasing the creative freedom that a strict programming grid never allowed.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: There's no gatekeeper telling you your episode has to be exactly forty-four minutes to fit around ad breaks.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: That said, podcasting has its own gatekeepers now too — algorithms, platform exclusives, the whole discoverability headache.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: So maybe it's less a story of radio dying and podcasts winning, and more a story of audio fragmenting into a dozen different habitats.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: Each one suited to a different mood: the car for radio, the commute or the gym for podcasts, and increasingly, video platforms for something in between.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: Whatever shape it takes, one thing hasn't changed — our appetite for a good voice telling us a good story.

script.speaker: Host
script.line: That's it for this segment. Next week, we'll be unpacking why vinyl refuses to die despite streaming dominating everything else.

lessons.title: Sunk Costs and the Trap of Bad Decisions

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Today we're tackling something deceptively simple but notoriously hard to internalize: the sunk cost fallacy.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: A sunk cost is money, time, or effort you've already spent, and crucially, cannot get back no matter what you decide going forward.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Classical economic theory says rational actors should ignore sunk costs entirely when making decisions about the future.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: And yet, virtually nobody does. We keep watching a terrible film because we've already sat through an hour of it.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: We keep funding a failing project because we've poured two years and half a million dollars into it already.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: The logic should be straightforward: that money is gone regardless. The only question that matters is whether continuing is the best use of future resources.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: But psychologically, walking away feels like admitting the original investment was wasted, and we're wired to avoid that admission at almost any cost.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: This is sometimes called escalation of commitment, and it's rampant in corporate settings, particularly among executives who greenlit the doomed project in the first place.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Their ego is entangled with the decision, so abandoning it isn't just a financial loss — it's a public admission of poor judgment.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Governments fall into this trap too. Think of infrastructure projects that balloon wildly over budget, yet nobody pulls the plug because so much has already been spent.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: There's a famous case, the Concorde supersonic jet, so notorious that economists sometimes call this the Concorde fallacy instead.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Both the British and French governments kept funding it well past the point of profitability, largely because withdrawing felt politically unthinkable.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Now, how do you guard against this in your own decision-making? First, separate the decision to continue from the decision that got you here.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: Ask yourself: if I were encountering this situation fresh today, with no history attached, would I choose to invest in it?

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: If the honest answer is no, that's your signal, however uncomfortable, that it's time to cut your losses.

script.speaker: Professor
script.line: For next week, I want you to find a real-world example of escalation of commitment — corporate, political, even personal — and be ready to dissect it.

lessons.title: Chasing the Monsoon Across the Deccan Plateau

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: There's a particular kind of stillness that settles over the Deccan Plateau just before the monsoon breaks.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: The air thickens, farmers glance skyward every few minutes, and even the cattle seem to sense that something is coming.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: We'd been tracking the storm system for nearly a week, driving from village to village, always seemingly one step behind it.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: Locals told us the same thing everywhere we went: when the monsoon finally arrives, it doesn't so much rain as detonate.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: And they weren't exaggerating. On the sixth day, the sky simply split open, and what had been dust turned to rivers within the hour.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: For farmers here, this isn't just weather — it's the difference between a harvest and a lost year, between feeding a family and going into debt.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: We met Sunita, who's farmed this same stretch of red soil for over thirty years, and she described the wait as almost unbearable.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: 'Every year,' she told us, 'we watch the sky like it owes us something.' It's a striking way to put it, and it stuck with me the entire trip.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: What's remarkable is how quickly the landscape transforms. Within days, parched fields turn a shade of green so vivid it looks almost artificial.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: Rivers that had been reduced to trickles suddenly surge, and roads we'd driven on the previous week become impassable within hours.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: We nearly lost the truck fording what had been a dry creek bed just three days earlier — a sobering reminder of how fast this landscape can turn against you.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: Climate scientists we spoke with are increasingly worried, though, that the monsoon's timing is growing less predictable year on year.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: A delay of even two or three weeks can devastate crop cycles that farmers have calibrated over generations.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: So while there's an undeniable beauty in watching the plateau come back to life, there's also an undercurrent of anxiety running through every conversation we had.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: The monsoon, for all its drama and spectacle, is ultimately a lifeline that millions of people can no longer take for granted.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.line: Next time, we follow that same water downstream, to the delta where the river finally meets the sea.
